Good world, bad gameplay. I'm not sure what you were thinking when you gave the player 1 energy per turn, but the emphasis on gnomes with mana means this constantly works against the player. You have the makings of a great game, but I won't support something that turns off players from their first run.

The art is fantastic, the gameplay feels good at first, but the cracks of this forcing you to replay "chapters" start to show. For every enemy there is a counter, however due to the random nature of a roguelike, you don't know which of those enemies shows up. The hero you start with has... okay cards, but you quickly find yourself debuffed to all heck. The counter? Immunity! However, that counter disables YOU from getting anything good. It blocks ALL debuffs on the hero, and ALL buffs as well. Okay, doesn't seem like that big of a problem right? Welp, there's a pigeon enemy who will ruin you if you want to have a build that doesn't really worry about mana, as they fill EVERY spot with a 14 hp pigeon. Every turn each of those pigeons gain 1 hp max and 1 extra damage. You'll quickly find yourself unable to deal with all three in a single turn and just be in this limbo of unable to win and unable to lose. Given that you CAN do things but every thing you CAN do is countered by something you need to use to counter other things enemies do against you? I cannot recommend this game to anyone who likes this style of game at this time. It goes out of its way to punish you for just not knowing, then further punishes you for knowing, trying to build to get past the boss at the end, but just having bad luck. 12 runs... I did 12 runs and through all of them I beat the first boss pretty handily, even the prologue the first time about, but only SAW the second boss once. If you want another reminder of how this game WANTS you to lose? Look at the achievements. There is one for losing at each of the bosses, as if they wanted to give you a participation medal for at least getting that far. "But didn't you say the bosses are hard and so to are the levels?" It so many words yes, however, when you, as the maker of this game, KNOW that you'll end up making people lose in the prologue, which in many games is the tutorial area... you're aiming to make people replay things again and again. TL;DR: If you like losing on repeat against things so outside your control, go for this demo and see if it too painful or not. If you don't like seeing that death just happens to like you, then don't look further than the art of this game.

If you look at the vast majority of the negative reviews they all complain about "1 mana per turn" or "the game is too difficult" As someone coming from ascension 20 slay the spire, it was refreshing to find a thoroughly challenging experience. The art is vibrant, and while i would appreciate a little diversity in runs, it was very entertaining. There are critiques to be had of this game, but "video game is too hard, therefore it is bad" is not a valid one. In fact, I replayed the entire game without using the skill tree systems at all. I don't mean to come across as snide, I just get upset when people bash a game with a lot of love put into it simply because it's difficult.
The Cypriot gaming industry is getting up from its knees, the interesting combat mechanics associated with the abilities on the cards are somewhat similar to the card wars of adventure time.

I think the game has a lot of potential, but suffers mainly from card balance and a few quirky design choices. A lot of the negative reviews complaining about the lack of mana probably didn't edit their starting decks, I had no issues with mana once changing my cards (mixing in free attack cards). I did not like the sausage mechanic at all. While I understand the need to potentially cap starting decks, the costs seem very arbitrary. Gold may be fairly accessible, but places to acquire sausages are not as frequent. The penalty of losing a single gnome isn't too bad, except if it is a crucial part of your deck. I am not sure if it was intended but being forced to take gnomes that are freed from the wagons (via loot spots) seems like a odd choice. I usually rejected gnomes when they didn't fit my deck, but the ones that come from loot spots seem to have no way to reject costing you sausage and deck bloat until you pay to remove them or hope they pass out.
I have never played a game like this and instantly enjoyed the battles along with the story. Very fun game and will play more!

The game has some interesting ideas that are marred by a variety of obviously terrible quality of life decisions, including but not limited to: A food system that is not intuitive, which punishes the player for adding cards to the roster and combines in a negative feedback loop to events that force new cards into your hand (most of which you don't want). An event system that is neat, but not apparent in its affect until you're already in a mission, an balance problems that absolutely wreck the experience as a whole. With work this title could be a 7/10, but it would take an entire rework of core systems to bring it any higher, as a result it's a pass for both players and my strong suggestion to the devs to launch, learn, and try again.

I liked the game since I enjoy the cartoon aesthetics but certain mechanics like dodge make the game really frustrating. Specifically on cases where the enemy uses the dodge ability, then attacks, and when the dodge status is about to run out they use it again. If it isn't removed then at least make the percentage of the dodge smaller and make it a bigger percentage for the hero through stacking combos of gnomes so it feels more fair. Moreover, maybe make the missions bigger for replayability kinda like how slay the spire does. Overall, would recommend the game but there are things that need polishing.

Union of Gnomes has so much potential, but the core issues in it's game design mean I can't see myself purchasing the full version. The Prologue is free, but only worth a try if you love cards games. The art is fun and vibrant, and I adore the character design. The mechanics are elaborate and interesting. I enjoyed the talent trees aspect. The trees for Miko and Roko give clear sign posts to potential deck builds. I tried poison and drunk slipper builds and found both quite entertaining. (The attributes I could take or leave, they seem like they need balancing - this is going to be a common theme). Contrary to popular opinion I found the mana mechanic with slow regen for Miko and none for Roko quite interesting, and the sausages are an interesting additional resource that fits thematically and I could see having potential to be a differentiator from Slay the Spire (a game this one is clearly heavily influenced by). However the game has huge balance issues and some serious design problems at it's core. The mechanics as they stand create negative feedback loops that leave you wondering how the game got to this state, and the balance is off to the point I hit a soft wall after the first 'campaign' level until I leveled up Miko enough to create a more powerful build. Yes I said create. This game fails at is core premise of being a rouge-lite deck builder. The game offers you gnome to add to your deck, but you'll almost never want to. As anyone familiar with deck building games should already know, larger decks have several inherent disadvantages. You draw through them slower which means you see every card in your deck less over a 'battle'. This weakens the impact of adding powerful cards, and reduces the change of drawing situational cards. There is a built in disadvantage to adding cards to your deck. Many games try to balance this by giving you a starting deck filled with weak cards, this encourages you to add the more powerful cards offered to you in a draft during the early stages of a run and helps ensure each run feels unique. Union of Gnomes does the opposite; almost every card/gnome you can encounter during a run is available when creating your starting deck, and the game punishes you for adding cards to your deck by increasing the sausage cost of your deck/wagon, with sausages being a very limited resource. These choices work to create a situation where you so heavily punished for adding any cards to you deck, that you'll never do it. I generally found myself adding at most 2 gnomes during a run, and generally only to balance the spread of card types because of the limitation of only having 1 of each copy in my starting deck. It's like the developers have borrowed mechanics from similar games with absolutely no understanding of why those mechanics worked in the original context. The level maps are another situation of borrowed befuddlement. There are 4 node types: Shop (Hideout/Sausage), Event (Quest/Scroll), Treasure (Event/Potion/Cage), and Battle. The map generation needs work desperately. It creates very limited levels, with nodes seldom intersecting and very few interesting decision points. I've had several levels that are essentially 3 paths with maybe 1 having a single decision point. The nodes are horrible balanced. Quests are neutral choices; they have positives and negatives outcomes, but can always be positive if you've seen them before and know which choices to select. Battles are neutral choices; they can cost you health or end a run, but rare guaranteed to reward gold (they also give cards, but as adding cards to your deck is horrible so you'll be skipping these). Technically they come in varieties, (normal, hard, deadly) but you can ignore that because the enemy balance is such that a hard battle is just as likely to take you out as a deadly. Treasure nodes are best avoided; they can give you gold, health, sausages, but they can also give you a dreaded cage which forces you to add useless cards to your deck. Shops are vital. You buy sausages, health, and upgrade cards. Importantly the cost to upgrade a cards increases exponentially so you'll want to hit every shop you possibly can. This reduces the map to "find the route with the most sausages, take that route" because nothing else really matters to the success of your run. You make every decision for the success of your run because the enemy balance is turned up to 11. Enemies will poison you, weaken you, all while hit you like a truck. The enemy scaling is brutal, Union of Gnomes: Prologue stays quick because if you aren't obliterating the enemies, you're dead. This creates yet another feedback loop to picking up new cards. Get it wrong and you run is quickly over. I'm optimistic though. The number of errors in the in game text makes it clear that this Prologue was rush and unpolished. The ideas are there, hopefully the devs will take the negative feedback as a sign the final game needs much, much more polish if it is to succeed. Overall I found Union of Gnomes: Prologue a fun, quirky, but often frustrating game. There are a few interesting decks to create and run through the gauntlet, but it completely fails as a rouge-lite deck builder.
局外自选卡牌组建套牌，所以你进入之前就卡组就已经成形了，完全不需要在战斗中拿卡，最多升级一下卡牌，而且无限升级、无限删卡，每次移动都会消耗香肠，所以选路线时多经过几个就可以了，完全不需要打小怪，太简单了吧。小偷那张卡太BUG了吧？小偷+毒奶无敌，可玩性目前只有2星，看不到重复玩的动力。

The art in the game looks wonderful. Game play is OK. Very similar to Slay the Spire and other similar style games. Seems to be a variety of cards that allow for different play styles. However, I have not played enough at this point to determine if some cards are must haves and others are wasted cards. My biggest complaint with the game is the sausage system. I understand the concept of having it. It adds a resource management component to the game that makes you want to balance your cards and choose your paths correctly. However, I have played numerous times where I went to an event space and was forced to take on 3 cards with not option to not take them. You get the unfortunate event of gaining 3 cards that might be useless and the unfortunate addition of 3 cards that will cost you 9 more sausages per movement up the path. You can purchase more sausages but they can cost you your ability to purchase anything else (card upgrades). Having to make this choice removes a bit of fun from the game. Some of the lower tiered fights can be harder than the boss or higher tiered fights. I recall beating 1 boss without taking any damage. Meanwhile a little girl with a broken bottle can usually can wipe me out or take me down to almost nothing.

I really wanted to like this game - I play Slay the Spire regularly (but never gotten past A3 and I'm not interested in doing so). I think unfortunately any deck-building rogue-like game will be compared to StS so would need to be really great and polished to do well. Pros: - graphics and premise are kinda nice - ability to customise the starting squad Cons: - really difficult to build synergies - many cards seem to have limited use (heal 8, apply 4 poison), although one can say that about some StS cards too - the sausage mechanic is confusing - unclear what happens when they run out, a whole level with two sausage points but at awkward places, not sure how much to buy ahead (and not always possible) - if I'm going into the shop / meeting point / encounter bonus etc, I expect to be able to leave the screen to check the map. In this game I exit that "stop" altogether. - the enemy intent is an icon, but I haven't been able to get the "description upon hover". Some are more obvious (heal), but the doll isn't. - feels like it drags on more than I can stand I might come back to this game in a bit, or try to have another go at beating the prologue, but I'm not sure I get this game as much as I do StS.

Union of Gnomes: Prologue is a charming entry into the card-based adventure genre, offering a whimsical experience that is sure to captivate players with its delightful graphics and engaging storyline. The game's presentation is top-notch, creating an enchanting world that is both inviting and fun to explore. Gameplay-wise, Union of Gnomes: Prologue is smooth and intuitive, making it accessible to players new to card games. However, the overall difficulty level might be a bit too low for more experienced gamers. While this makes the game approachable, it can also lead to a lack of challenge that may leave some players wanting more. A bit more complexity and difficulty would make the game more satisfying for a broader audience. The achievement system in Union of Gnomes: Prologue is another area that could use some refinement. Currently, the game includes achievements for losing against bosses, which feels counterproductive. Achievements should ideally reward skillful play and strategic victories, rather than commemorating defeats. Revamping the achievement system to better reflect player accomplishments would greatly enhance the sense of progression and satisfaction. Additionally, the variety of cards available in the game is somewhat limited. Introducing more cards would provide a richer experience, allowing players to experiment with different strategies and playstyles. This would not only add depth to the game but also increase its replay value, keeping players engaged over a longer period. In summary, Union of Gnomes: Prologue is a delightful and accessible card game that shows a lot of promise. Its captivating visuals and approachable gameplay make it a joy to play, but there is room for improvement in terms of difficulty and card variety. With some tweaks and additions, it has the potential to become a standout title in the genre. For now, it remains an enjoyable experience that hints at even greater things to come.

I saw this game on YouTube described as a Slay The Spire killer, and brother, this isn't that game. It has some interesting design choices. Your mana (energy) doesn't automatically refill each round, you need to play the correct type of gnome to add mana back. Yes, some gnomes do not require mana to play, so maybe that's not so bad. But there is another resource everyone has mentioned: sausages. As you traverse the map, you need to feed your gnomes. And surprise, surprise, the more powerful gnomes need to eat more sausages. So this design removes choice from the player to add what I think is an artificial level of difficulty. To the get gud bros, it's fun to explore the mechanics of games I enjoy (StS, Balatro) to indeed try and get gud. But brother, this game ain't it.

After playing for a few hours, I found myself thoroughly enjoying "Union of Gnomes: Prologue." Rescuing my fellow gnome buddies from the evil clutches of Snow White was entertaining and kept me coming back for more. https://blkhertgameviews.com/

The game is really fun, but I'm quite convinced that the third chapter boss is not beatable without tedious efforts over and over again. I've played through the other two chapters over and over to get XP for leveling my character up. However, even with almost all of the extra skills unlocked and over 20 extra points added... The third chapter boss still wins every single time. I tried many different card layouts and I had a good build, but I still had lost. I've yet to beat it and the only thing I can do is keep playing for XP to add more skill points. The problem is that you only get 3 for completing a level and the amount of XP jumps exponentially each time. It's just really tedious and downright ridiculous as you could never beat this chapter with the standard character and card layout. I'd still recommend it, because the game is free and fun to play.

This game is awesome, and far above what I would expect from a free game. I'm close to 2 hours in and still have much progression to unlock. I see negative reviews about mana, but personally I call that hogwash. The starter character regenerates 1 mana per turn and the game is not very punishing. You don't lose all your progression on death, just have to replay whatever mission you died on basically. 5/5 for me.

The only specific thing I didn't like was the sausage game mechanic that the game could really do without. It doesn't add anything and my gnomes seem to die at a rate of knots towards the end of a run. There's nothing else about it that's terrible but there is also a glut of games exactly like this. They're pumping out roguelikes and deckbuilders at such a rate, I'm not speaking hyperbole here when I say I see 2+ brand new games similar to this every week. So if it is not amazing, I simply pass.

There's already quite a bit of content here in this prologue. I think I would like to see a bit more variety and inventiveness in both cards/events... to be able to use some more strategies and the same with enemies. But even as it is now it's already very enjoyable and feels like the basis of a very good game.

Wow. Great start. This could be a gem. TLDR: Depends how much depth the final game has. PROs: Epic settings & graphics style. Seriously whoever the artist is should get at least half the profits from this game. Incredible art hands down. Sound is decent. Controls work well. Tactics seems fairly fun and unique. I assume it will be replayable too since the stage's layout changes each time you enter. CONs: Sometimes the wording on cards makes in very confusing which character the card will target. Should be an easy fix. The Pigeon Monster. Worst part of the game by far. Its, just... not... fun. Boring as all heck to fight a dinky monster that can summon two of its friends every single round so you can barely ever get a chance to take a swipe at the final pigeon and end the fight. On top of creating endless clones, it heals itself. So you can spend twenty minutes carefully dispensing endless pigeons just in order to lower the final pigeons life close enough you may win, then round 80 it decides to heal itself full life and you get to start over. Absolutely broken mechanic. I'm sure there are very specific builds that can help you counter this endless spawn / heal combo, but honestly it feels like you shouldn't be forced into one team composition to address one specific monster type. I typically enjoy having to adjust my tactics for different maps / situations. Thinking and changing strategy is fun. The pigeon monster is not. Its tedious and annoying. You are basically just waiting on the luck of RNG. Silly. Okay that being said, as long as this gets properly game tested to avoid frustrating battles that never end, I think this game is going good places.

A solid roguelite deckbuilder with a lot of charm. The game feels very much like Slay the Spire, but with some noticeable differences. You keep armor at the end of your turn, allowing both you and your enemies to stockpile your defenses. There are also a whole lot of status conditions, as well as a level-up system to provide some meta progression. For the main game, though, one strategy seems to be the clear best, which is poison. Just poison everybody until they die, and most status effects no longer hurt you. Miko is also way better than the other captain, since Miko refreshes mana at the start of each turn. The other guy doesn't, making him almost useless long term. He's also way worse at poison. I have mixed feelings on the sausage mechanic where you need to keep your resources stocked to travel. It essentially forces you to micromanage your deck so you can keep moving, but since you can't get rid of troops easily, it usually results in you not taking any gnome rewards. Whether you think this is a good thing or not is up to you, but I wasn't the biggest fan. The game's general balance system is good though (if you're using Miko) and the art style is gorgeous.

游戏无聊就算了还有BUG，假如你44滴血进入战斗，还有22滴血的时候你因为事情退出了游戏，等你再次进入游戏并继续战斗的时候，你竟然是以22滴血开始战斗，而敌人全部都是满状态，这bug给我看笑了（？事件打3伐木工的时候出现的这种情况）。而且游戏操作一点也不平滑，地图界面滚轮移动的距离聊胜于无，逼着你只能用左键长按拖动地图。然后每次选择关卡进入战斗的时候还有一个确认键，这地方加个确认是干啥呢？别人是只有特殊情况才特意弹确认提醒（比如pvz里面没带向日葵进入战斗），你这打一把弹一下打一把弹一下是何意味呢？接着卡牌拖动不够丝滑，而且每次必须要拖到目标才能选中打出。你学别人杀戮尖塔怎么只学其表层不学它的精华？我举个例子，你只能给角色自己释放的卡牌（比如获得能量的牌），你卡牌只要往上移就可以打出，这样多方便，你非要挪到你角色那里才能打出。卡牌的打击感和反馈一般，音效也一般，这个我就不多说了。总而言之就是一款无聊的作品，鉴于现在还是demo，制作组继续打磨吧。
